title: A test across grades must adapt
statement: A test that must measure learners across several grades should adapt to each one, since a fixed form of normal length spread over that range is imprecise everywhere.
example: One assessment design rejected a fixed 40-item form because it could not measure readers from grade 2 to grade 5 with a standard error of 4 or less.
detail: The validity BrainLift of an interim reading assessment for grades 2 to 5 holds that a fixed 40-item form cannot measure scores from about 161 to 227, from the fall of grade 2 to the spring of grade 5, with a standard error of 4 or less, because items informative for a struggling grade-2 reader are noise for an advanced grade-5 reader; an earlier fixed-form design was superseded on the record for this reason (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/00_BRAINLIFT.md`, line 49). Its argument is arithmetic: information concentrates where an item's difficulty is near the learner's ability, and 40 items spread across a 6.5-logit range leave too little anywhere, which is why the published test it mirrors is adaptive too (line 51). It qualifies the record that spreads a test's items across easy, medium and hard: over several grades, even a spread fixed form is thin at every level.
against: The argument assumes a 40-item length and a target error of 4 or less, and it is reasoned from measurement theory rather than measured on these learners.

evidence.quote: A fixed 40-item form cannot measure RIT ~161–227 (G2 fall through G5 spring) with SEM ≤ 4: items informative for a struggling G2 reader are noise for an advanced G5 reader.
this is arithmetic, not preference — Fisher information concentrates near |θ − b| ≈ 0, and 40 items spread across a 6.5-logit range leaves too little information anywhere.
